candidate_pool: exact frozen dense top20; no candidate additions/removals in valid B or C

context.admission: total estimate + output reservation <= total limit AND every pair estimate + output reservation <= pair limit
context.estimator: canonical serialized UTF-8 bytes plus overhead; provisional conservative estimate, not native Jev tokens
context.pair_estimator: same state plus one full question/rubric under its actual question ID and model wrapper, plus overhead
context.truncation_caveat: Any truncation is required by this conservative byte-based admission policy, not proven necessary under the unpublished native tokenizer.

truncation_policy.activation: only when one complete candidate exceeds either conservative admission limit
truncation_policy.algorithm: retain the longest Unicode-codepoint prefix of original skill_md that fits both limits; remove only its right suffix; no marker, normalization, rewriting, or label-based selection
truncation_policy.batching: greedy original dense order; split before exceeding either limit; full text remains unchanged when its individual request fits
truncation_policy.minimum_body: at least one non-whitespace character from the original skill_md
truncation_policy.name: truncate_skill_md_right
truncation_policy.unavoidable_failure: block the whole selected query if immutable content plus a nonempty body cannot fit; never skip or substitute candidates

rows.query: Our team maintains an open-source MIDI automation toolkit called "docent" on GitHub, and we've gotten a flood of new issues after our last release. I need two things: First, can you go through the open issues in our tracker and triage them — categorize by severity (critical bug, enhancement, question, duplicate), assign priority labels, identify which ones are related to our MMD parser vs. the runtime engine, and flag any that should be closed as duplicates or out-of-scope? Second, one of the bug reports (#247) includes a broken `.mmd` file that a user says causes a validation error. They're trying to create a generative ambient sequence with nested loops, pitch bend sweeps from 0 to 8192 over 16 bars, random velocity values between 40-110 on each note, and CC#1 modulation that ramps up during each loop iteration. Can you write a corrected version of that MMD file with proper syntax, making sure the timing paradigm is set correctly, the loop counters don't conflict, and the sweep/random directives are valid? I want to include the fixed file in our response to the issue and also reference it in a new "examples" section of our docs.

Hey, I run a small indie game studio and we have about 15 Discord channels across three servers (dev-general, art-team, backend-eng, playtesting-feedback, bug-reports, etc.). I was out for the past week dealing with a family emergency and I'm completely lost on what happened. Can you pull together a consolidated recap of all the important discussions, decisions, blockers, and announcements from the last 7 days across all three servers? I'd love it broken down by server and channel, with highlights of any action items or unresolved debates so I can jump back in without making everyone repeat themselves.

I just opened a PR (#247) on our "HarborSync" Kotlin/Ktor maritime logistics API repo — it refactors the vessel tracking module to use coroutines and migrates from Exposed to Jetbrains' new Kotlin DataFrame for the analytics endpoints. Can you review my PR, flag anything critical like concurrency bugs or API contract breaks, and then go ahead and fix whatever issues you find?

We're about to cut the v3.2.0 release of our `~/repos/chartforge` library (a TypeScript charting toolkit). Can you bump the version from 3.1.4 to 3.2.0 everywhere it appears — `package.json`, `package-lock.json`, the `--version` flag output in `src/cli.ts`, the "Current Version" badge and installation instructions in `README.md`, and the version references in `docs/getting-started.md` and `docs/changelog.md`? We're not publishing to npm yet, just getting all the files aligned so QA can verify the release candidate.

Our compliance team at "ShieldComm" is building a multi-channel alert system for our security operations center — when our SIEM detects a threat event classified at different severity levels (based on our Documentation Robotics Security Layer model that categorizes incidents into zones like perimeter, application, and data layers), we need to dispatch notifications via Twilio SMS and voice calls to on-call responders with escalation paths. The tricky part: we want to prototype three different escalation strategies simultaneously — one that fans out all alerts immediately, one that uses a tiered delay with SMS first then voice fallback, and one that routes based on the specific security layer the threat was detected in — and compare them side by side before picking a winner. Can you help me set up the Twilio integration with proper rate limiting and opt-in compliance, define the security layer classification schema that maps threat severity to notification urgency and channel selection, and structure the whole thing using git worktrees so we can develop and test all three escalation approaches in parallel branches without them stomping on each other? We're using Node.js/TypeScript and want to be able to checkpoint each branch independently so we can mix-and-match the best parts later.

Can you review the new dashboard interface our junior dev built for "AquaFlow," our water utility monitoring platform? Here's the Figma link and the deployed staging URL — I want a thorough audit covering visual hierarchy, spacing consistency, color contrast ratios against WCAG 2.1 AA, responsive behavior across breakpoints (mobile/tablet/desktop), touch target sizing, keyboard navigation order, focus indicator visibility, loading state treatments, and whether our data visualization cards follow our existing component library patterns. Please produce a prioritized report with severity levels so we know what to fix before the stakeholder demo on Thursday.

Hey, I'm building a new REST API for our internal employee directory service at `~/repos/staff-directory`. The stack is Node.js, Express, and TypeScript with a PostgreSQL database accessed through Knex. I need you to scaffold the full backend for a "departments" resource — that means the route definitions, a controller that handles request/response concerns, a service layer for business logic (like preventing deletion of a department that still has employees assigned), and a repository layer for all DB queries. Each department has an `id`, `name`, `description`, `manager_id` (FK to employees), and `created_at`. I also need: (1) input validation middleware using Zod for the create and update endpoints, (2) a centralized async error handler middleware so controllers don't need try/catch everywhere, (3) proper HTTP status codes including 409 for duplicate department names and 422 for validation failures, and (4) integration tests using Supertest and an in-memory PG instance via `pg-mem` that cover the happy paths plus the conflict and validation error cases. Please make sure the layers are clearly separated — controllers should never import Knex directly, and services shouldn't touch `req`/`res` objects.

Our team just launched a new multi-step checkout flow for our e-commerce platform "CartBloom" — it spans a React frontend, a Node.js BFF layer, and a Stripe payment microservice. We need a comprehensive Playwright end-to-end test suite that covers the full happy path (browse → add to cart → enter shipping → apply promo code → pay → confirmation page) plus key failure scenarios like expired promo codes, payment declines, and session timeouts. The tricky parts: the shipping address form uses a Google Places autocomplete widget, the promo code triggers an async validation call that can take 2-3 seconds, and the Stripe payment confirmation redirects through a 3D Secure iframe before landing on our confirmation page. We also want to make sure tests work reliably in CI where things are slower — right now our prototype tests are super flaky because they use hard waits and fragile CSS selectors. Can you write out the test structure with proper page object models, ARIA-based selectors, smart retry/assertion patterns, and a data factory that seeds test users and promo codes via our admin API before each run?

Hey, I'd like to create and publish a Ruby gem called `schema_drift` that detects and reports database schema differences between environments (dev, staging, production). I need help setting up the full gem structure with Bundler, writing the gemspec with proper metadata and dependency declarations, organizing the lib directory with a clean module hierarchy, adding a version file following semantic versioning (starting at 0.1.0), configuring RSpec for testing with a solid test suite covering the core diff logic, setting up YARD for documentation generation, and finally walking me through the steps to build and publish it to RubyGems.org. Can you scaffold the whole thing out with actual code?

Our Swift SDK "ContractKit" auto-generates signed PDF contracts (using pdf-lib for form filling and DocuSign for e-signatures) whenever a deal closes in our CRM, and we just added a new `ContractAssemblyAgent` that calls the Anthropic Claude API to dynamically choose which clause templates to include based on deal metadata. I need two things: first, help me build the pipeline that takes the agent's structured output (selected clauses, party details, effective dates) and assembles a multi-page PDF with filled form fields, appended exhibits, and a DocuSign envelope for routing — and second, I need to record the actual Anthropic HTTP request/response traffic (including the streaming SSE chunks from Claude when it returns the clause selections and tool call results) so I can generate paste-ready Swift fixtures for our `ReplayHTTPClient`-based unit tests in the ContractAssemblyAgent test suite. The recordings should cover the happy path (all clauses selected), a partial-selection edge case, and a structured output with tool calls for fetching party info. Can you walk me through both pieces end to end?

rubric: Irrelevant — does not meaningfully satisfy the request.
Weak match — shares some topic or functionality but would not adequately solve the request.
Partial match — useful for part of the request but incomplete or missing an important requirement.
Strong match — directly addresses the request with only minor limitations.
Excellent match — directly and comprehensively matches the requested capability.
score_mapping: Five ordered criteria; native continuous score 0..4; displayed relevance=native+1
selection: SHA256(query_id UTF-8), ascending hex digest then query_id; smoke is first10 of pilot200
version_policy: Every response records a non-alias actual model; one actual version per ingested comparison.
